candidates.title: Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neurons (DAWIN): A Universal Primitive for Continuous-Time Spatiotemporal Learning
candidates.content: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural layers in MLPs, Transformers, and graph neural networks. DAWIN couples spatial projection with elapsed-time-dependent wave excitation and integrates it into a local complex state through closed-form damped evolution, avoiding numerical differential equation solvers. We show that DAWIN generalizes static sinusoidal and memoryless wave neurons on interval-augmented inputs, derive closed-form gradients, and establish bounded-input bounded-output stability for positive damping and sampling intervals bounded away from zero. An associative Triton prefix-scan implementation, DAWINLinear, uses FP32 accumulation and achieves O(log L) parallel depth for sequence length L. Across 11 parameter-matched tasks covering irregular oscillators, MuJoCo dynamics, pedestrian trajectories, and PhysioNet 2012 clinical sequences, DAWIN outperforms Neural CDE on 9 tasks and ReLU-MLP on 8. It achieves the lowest error on dense clinica

candidates.title: BiSAT: Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization for Speech Language Models
candidates.content: Speech language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens. Their tokenizer must therefore preserve both acoustic detail and linguistic content at a low bitrate. Semantic-enhanced tokenizers may lose acoustic detail, whereas acoustic-oriented tokenizers retain acoustic variation that makes language modeling harder. Unified tokenizers combine both, but representing acoustic detail and linguistic content within a single feature space can cause interference between the two objectives, and existing approaches typically align acoustic representations to fixed semantic targets from a frozen teacher. We propose Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization (BiSAT), a unified tokenization framework with separate acoustic and semantic branches aligned by a shared-index mechanism. This design learns acoustic and semantic representations in separate continuous spaces while producing a single discrete code sequence, and it jointly optimizes both encoders without relying on fixed semantic teacher targets. Based on BiSAT, we develop BiSAT-TTS, a zero-shot text-to-speech system comprising an autoregressive text-speech LM and a conditional flow-matching acoustic decoder.

candidates.title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries
candidates.content: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. candidates.title: MGMem: An Efficient, Deterministic, and Provenance-Preserving Framework for Long-Horizon Agent Memory
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.33174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents need persistent memory that surfaces the right past interaction at the right time across thousands of turns. Many systems index by invoking generative LLMs to rewrite history into summaries, facts, or knowledge graphs--a step that is (a) costly (thousands of generative calls per build), (b) non-deterministic (undermining reproducibility and giving inconsistent answers across runs), and (c) provenance-erasing (the reader sees synthesized text, not the original turn). We propose MGMem, a framework with no generative indexing calls that replaces this step with a deterministic discriminative-parser pipeline: recurring mentions across sessions are organized into an incidence graph, question mentions are resolved by a subject-conditioned three-stage resolver, and raw dialogue episodes are returned to the reader. On English multi-session dialogue QA, MGMem outperforms matched-protocol baselines on LoCoMo without generative indexing calls; on the full LongMemEval-S, it remains competitive overall and leads or ties on single-session types among local retrieval comparisons. The goal of this clinical trial is to investigate whether administering a probiotic (Infloran®) to infants who received antibiotics in the first 28 days of life can restore or enhance their immune response to routine vaccines. Antibiotic use in the first weeks of life can lower the levels of beneficial gut bacteria, such as bifidobacteria, which play a key role in immune function. candidates.title: SAFE (Self-Administration of Flumist to ImprovE Uptake: A Household-Based Cluster Randomized Trial)
candidates.content: [PHASE4] RECRUITING | 申办方/赞助方: McMaster University | 适应症: Influenza (Healthy Volunteers). The flu is a health risk for Canadians. It causes up to 15,000 hospitalizations every year and is one of the top 10 causes of death. Getting a flu vaccine is the best way to prevent the flu and any severe complications. Unfortunately, many Canadians do not get the flu vaccine. A recent survey found that less than a quarter of healthy adults got the flu vaccine. In Canada, current standard access to influenza vaccination is at physician offices, public health clinics, or pharmacy. Therefore, this study is testing a novel access route to influenza vaccine. This study will answer the question: "Will self-administration at home of FLUMIST through a pharmacy pick up model increase uptake of influenza vaccination compared to usual care?" FLUMIST is a needle-free vaccine given as a nasal spray. Households will be randomly chosen to either be offered the FLUMIST vaccine that can be given at home or to make their own choice for the flu season, which may or may not include vaccination.

candidates.title: Signs, Both Clinical and Poetic
candidates.content: In medicine, a sign is a patently observable manifestation of disease, such as jaundice or tremor. The poem “Signs” plays on the recognizable signification of illness, asking what happens when evidence of societal ills is everywhere in public view, but without diagnosis or remedy to follow. The anaphora of denial of the opening stanza, emblazoned on a literal sign posted on a clinic’s front door, first announces medicine’s constraints in treating the societal breakdown whose disease-like symptoms are so plainly seen. Yet other signs of malaise, perhaps more visible via poetry, abound elsewhere: a placard advertises free naloxone on a bench upon which an apparently unhoused man sleeps, or “ODs,” while on a street corner another man’s hand-scrawled sign implores “Homeless. Anything helps.” These accumulating, ironically numerous clinical and poetic signs seem to point to an overarching sign of absence, symbolized by the “makeshift memorial” (with its own signs and messages we can easily imagine) on the same street corner for another unhoused person who, like it, has disappeared. candidates.title: George Whitesides, 1939-2026
candidates.content: George Whitesides, whose name will be familiar to generations of chemists, biochemists, chemical biologists and many others, has recently passed away at the age of 87. He was an extremely accomplished scientist who worked in an extraordinarily diverse number of fields over his long career, and he was also a very prolific author, mentor, and speaker. I had occasion to interact with him several times over the years and I enjoyed these contacts a great deal - he had a unusually wide-ranging intelligence and curiosity that the world definitely needs more of. Whitesides began his career at MIT in the early 60s and moved to Harvard in 1982, where he stayed. It is very difficult to summarize his research accomplishments, because he moved from field to field far more often than is typical for most scientists - indeed, it’s been remarked by many people over the years that this was surely a factor in his never receiving a Nobel Prize, because it was so hard to point to the specific area to cite. candidates.title: We're Getting Less Demented. Why?
candidates.content: Here’s a fact that I don’t think that a lot of people are aware of: the risks of developing dementia with aging have been falling pretty steadily for a long time now in the industrialized world. This trend has been holding for decades now. An 80-year-old today is much less likely to show signs of dementia (memory loss, confusion, etc.) than the people in their parents’ generation. (Some may be reminded of the similar Flynn Effect, which is likely to have some similar drivers behind it). Now that is good news, but we scientific types are not content with that. No, we would very much like to know where this good news is coming from and why. That’s the focus of this new paper, which is looking into a fundamental question: do people reaching old age today have higher cognitive capacity to start with (presumably built up in their younger years), or are they holding on to it better as they age? Those aren’t mutually exclusive, either, of course. And we have to assume that these effects must be due to environmental and behavioral changes, since this is far, far too short a time to see much of a genetic-background change. candidates.title: DNA Damage and Lifespan
candidates.content: One of the indisputable results in aging research is that caloric restriction (CR) increases lifespan. This was discovered in mice back in the 1930s, and in the decades since this result has been repeated many times and extended to a whole list of other species, and by that I mean from yeast all the way to primates. It’s an impressively broad result, but it has reason to be: individuals of all of these species age and eventually die, all of them of course eat to survive, and they all use basically the same metabolic pathways to produce metabolic energy from that food. And we all carry the same general sorts of biomolecules around in our cells, with each cell holding its irreplaceable cargo of DNA information. Insofar as we breathe oxygen, convert our food to ATP, and guard the integrity of our DNA, we are brothers to yeast and to every other living creature on the planet. But for an effect this striking we still have a lot of blank spots in our understanding of it, and this new paper seems to have uncovered another one. candidates.title: Defining the role of RNase E in the mycobacterial degradosome-like network
candidates.content: Abstract Messenger RNA (mRNA) degradation is a fundamentally important process that is regulated in response to stress in the globally important pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis . Several mycobacterial ribonucleases (RNases) are hypothesized to function together to coordinate mRNA degradation, but the interactions among them are mostly undefined. One of the rate-limiting enzymes, RNase E, contains intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Here, we have defined the interactions among major mycobacterial mRNA degradation enzymes and identified the functions of the two IDRs of RNase E in the nonpathogenic model Mycolicibacterium smegmatis . We found that the two IDRs differentially impact mRNA degradation rates in vivo but are largely functionally redundant in their impact on steady-state transcript abundance. In vitro , the IDRs are uninvolved in catalysis but play major roles in RNA binding and interactions with other mRNA degradation enzymes, namely PNPase, RNase J, and RhlE1, including stimulation of the ATPase activity of RhlE1. candidates.title: Chromosome folding and segregation defects in a class A PBP mutant of Bacillus subtilis
candidates.content: Abstract Most bacterial cells have at least one class A penicillin-binding protein (aPBP) that plays a key role in cell wall (peptidoglycan) synthesis. It is generally assumed that peptidoglycan synthesis activity constitutes the primary, if not the only, function of aPBPs. Loss of PBP1, the major aPBP of Bacillus subtilis , results in a mild morphogenic phenotype in which cells are thinner and longer than normal. The increased length was thought to be responsible for an increase in the number of nucleoids per cell. However, we now show that ponA mutants, which lack PBP1, have a chromosome segregation defect. The defect appears to occur because the reduced cell diameter impacts chromosome architecture. The increased cell length probably arises because the chromosome abnormality occludes cell division sites. The main consequence of the altered chromosome arrangement seems to be a specific defect in chromosome segregation, characterized by increased chromosome dimer formation, as inactivation of the XerCD- dif system in ponA mutants leads to severe chromosome segregation and growth defects. candidates.title: The Updateable Human Virome Database and toolkit: a novel framework for human virome analysis
candidates.content: Abstract Current computational methods for analyzing viruses in human metagenomes rely on static databases composed largely of fragmented virus genomes, which are mostly derived from gastrointestinal samples. This issue limits the identification of viruses exclusively found outside the gastrointestinal tract and impairs analyses requiring high-quality genomes. To address these issues, we created the Updateable Human Virome Database (UHVDB), an expandable database of 1.15 million high-quality, clustered, and annotated virus genomes integrated from pre-existing human virome databases and diverse human sample metagenome assemblies. We developed an associated toolkit that enables users to (i) update UHVDB by mining, clustering, and annotating virus sequences, (ii) taxonomically profile viruses in metagenomes and metatranscriptomes, (iii) estimate phage replication activity using phage-to-host ratios, and (iv) determine the genomic characteristics of detected viruses.
